The number \(6.02 \times 10^{23}\) is called Avogadro's number, the number of representative particles in a mole. It is an experimentally determined number. A representative particle is the smallest unit in which a substance naturally exists. For the majority of elements, the representative particle is the atom. Iron, carbon, and helium consist of iron atoms, carbon atoms, and helium atoms, respectively. Seven elements exist in nature as diatomic molecules and they are \(\ce{H_2}\), \(\ce{N_2}\), \(\ce{O_2}\), \(\ce{F_2}\), \(\ce{Cl_2}\), \(\ce{Br_2}\), and \(\ce{I_2}\). The representative particle for these elements is the molecule. Likewise, all molecular compounds such as \(\ce{H_2O}\) and \(\ce{CO_2}\) exist as molecules and so the molecule is their representative particle. For ionic compounds such as \(\ce{NaCl}\) and \(\ce{Ca(NO_3)_2}\), the representative particle is the formula unit. A mole of any substance contains Avogadro's number \(\left( 6.02 \times 10^{23} \right)\) of representative particles. The behavior follows from the kinetic theory of gases, which describes gas particles as moving continuously and spreading throughout their available space. At ordinary conditions where gases behave approximately ideally, the volume depends on the number of particles, temperature, and pressure rather than on the chemical identity of the gas alone. Real gases can deviate from ideal behavior, especially at high pressures or low temperatures, when molecular attractions and the finite sizes of particles become more significant. Avogadro’s law is useful for understanding gas reactions, calculating gas volumes, and interpreting laboratory measurements. It also illustrates how a simple relationship between particle count and measurable volume emerges from the collective behavior of enormous numbers of molecules. How Avogadro’s number differs from Avogadro’s constant The terms Avogadro’s number and Avogadro’s constant are often used interchangeably in introductory chemistry, but there is a technical distinction. Avogadro’s number is the numerical value 6.02214076 × 10²³. Avogadro’s constant, represented by Nₐ, is that value expressed per mole: Nₐ = 6.02214076 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ The unit

Because sodium chloride consists of an extended arrangement of ions rather than separate NaCl molecules, describing a mole of sodium chloride in terms of formula units is more accurate. The central idea behind Avogadro’s number Avogadro’s number provides a bridge between the microscopic and macroscopic worlds. Individual atoms and molecules determine the properties and behavior of substances, but scientists usually work with samples that contain enormous numbers of those particles. By defining one mole as exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³ specified entities, chemistry gains a consistent counting unit that can be linked to mass, volume, concentration, and chemical reactions. The number itself does not explain why atoms bond, why reactions occur, or why materials have particular properties. Instead, it supplies the essential quantitative connection that allows scientists to relate those microscopic processes to observable measurements. That connection is why Avogadro’s number remains one of the most important foundations of chemistry. It turns the seemingly impossible task of counting individual particles into a practical system for measuring matter and predicting how substances behave.

Knowing the concentration of a substance helps scientists determine how much of it is present in a solution and how it may interact with other molecules. The mole connects these concentrations to the numbers of particles involved. In environmental science, chemists measure substances such as dissolved oxygen, pollutants, and greenhouse gases. A dozen is useful for counting everyday objects, while a mole is useful for counting the extraordinarily large numbers of particles found in ordinary amounts of matter. Even a tiny grain of material can contain an immense number of atoms, making direct counting impractical. The particles represented by a mole depend on what is being measured. History [edit] Origin of the concept [edit] The Avogadro constant is named after the Italian scientist Amedeo Avogadro (1776–1856), who, in 1811, first proposed that the volume of a gas (at a given pressure and temperature) is proportional to the number of atoms or molecules regardless of the nature of the gas.[12] Avogadro's hypothesis was popularized four years after his death by Stanislao Cannizzaro, who advocated Avogadro's work at the Karlsruhe Congress in 1860.[13] The name Avogadro's number was coined in 1909 by the physicist Jean Perrin, who defined it as the number of molecules in exactly 32 grams of oxygen gas.[14] This definition numerically equates the mass of a mole of a substance, in grams, to the mass of one molecule relative to the mass of a hydrogen atom. Because of the law of definite proportions, the mass of a hydrogen atom was the natural unit of atomic mass and was assumed to be 1/16 of the atomic mass of oxygen. Back in the early 1900s, marketing and advertising were a lot simpler — think print ads in newspapers and door-to-door sales. Then came the 1950s, and television entered the scene. Suddenly, brands could tell their stories with a little flair. Fast forward to today, and we’re in the age of search engines, social media, and AI-driven strategies. Marketing and advertising campaigns have become smarter, faster, and more personalized — but also more complex. Marketing and advertising often get lumped together, but they’re not the same. Mixing them up is like using salt when you need sugar — it won’t give you the result you were hoping for. Understanding the difference helps businesses strike the right balance between the big-picture strategy of marketing and the direct approach of advertising. What is marketing? passages_top20.text: Discover the differences between marketing and advertising and how each relates to modern business As technology continues to evolve and grow in importance, modern businesses employ diverse marketing and advertising strategies to reach potential customers and close sales. Stretching from traditional media to digital marketing online and in social media, marketing and advertising seem to be everywhere. Part of this reality is due to the effectiveness of marketing and advertising strategies in driving success for companies of every shape and size. While sometimes used interchangeably, there are actually many differences between marketing and advertising. In basic terms, marketing is the process of identifying customer needs and determining how best to meet those needs. In contrast, advertising is the exercise of promoting a company and its products or services through paid channels. In other words, advertising is a component of marketing. But the differences do not end there. What Is Marketing and Why Is It Important? Marketing is a business practice that involves identifying, predicting and meeting customer needs. passages.text: Renaissance Europe · c. 1440–1455 How Did the Printing Press Change the World? Johannes Gutenberg's movable-type printing press, developed in Mainz, Germany around 1440–1450, let books be mass-produced for the first time in history, collapsing the cost of a book by roughly 95% within decades. That triggered an information explosion: an estimated 20 million books were printed in Europe by 1500 alone, fueling the spread of literacy, the Protestant Reformation, and the Scientific Revolution — while Gutenberg himself, ruined by legal disputes, never profited from his own invention. Frequently asked questions Did Gutenberg invent printing itself? Not entirely — woodblock printing had existed in China and Korea for centuries before Gutenberg, and Korea had even experimented with metal movable type earlier. Gutenberg's specific innovation was a complete, efficient system for European alphabets: durable, precisely-cast reusable metal type, oil-based ink that adhered to metal, and a reliable mechanical press — combined into a practical, scalable process that transformed European printing specifically. Did Gutenberg get rich from his invention? No — one of history's great ironies. His financial backer, Johann Fust, sued him for loan repayment right as his masterwork, the Gutenberg Bible, was nearing completion around 1455, and a court awarded Fust the printing business and equipment. Once printing became established, corrected editions of classical works could be reproduced in substantial quantities and distributed across European intellectual networks. Scholars could more easily compare editions and develop shared references to particular texts. Latin remained an important scholarly language, but printing also encouraged the growth of vernacular literature in languages such as Italian, German, French, Spanish and English. Writers could reach audiences beyond their immediate locality. Printing therefore helped transform the intellectual geography of Europe by making scholarly and literary materials more portable and reproducible. It did not eliminate manuscript culture, which continued for centuries, but it shifted the balance between handwritten and mechanically reproduced texts. The printing press was particularly important for religious communication and the Protestant Reformation. Martin Luther's criticisms of Church practices, sermons, theological arguments and translations of biblical material could be reproduced and distributed rapidly through pamphlets, broadsheets and books. Other reformers also used printing to communicate their ideas. Catholic authorities responded with their own printed works, polemics and catechetical materials. Printing did not cause the Reformation by itself because religious disputes, political interests, theological developments and institutional grievances already existed. Before the mid fifteenth century, most European books were copied by hand, which made production relatively slow and expensive. Mechanical printing allowed printers to create multiple copies from the same typeset text, reducing the marginal labour required for additional copies. The technology did not immediately make books cheap or universal, but it changed the economics of publishing and gradually expanded the availability of written material. Printing shops emerged across European cities, producing religious works, classical texts, legal documents, schoolbooks, calendars, pamphlets and commercial information. This increased circulation of texts affected education, religion, scholarship, politics, administration and commerce. The printing press was therefore not merely a faster way to make books; it altered the infrastructure through which European societies produced, preserved and distributed knowledge. Printing had a major effect on Renaissance humanism. Humanist scholars sought manuscripts of Greek and Roman authors, edited texts and circulated their interpretations. passages.text: Renaissance Europe · c. 1440–1455 How Did the Printing Press Change the World? Johannes Gutenberg's movable-type printing press, developed in Mainz, Germany around 1440–1450, let books be mass-produced for the first time in history, collapsing the cost of a book by roughly 95% within decades. That triggered an information explosion: an estimated 20 million books were printed in Europe by 1500 alone, fueling the spread of literacy, the Protestant Reformation, and the Scientific Revolution — while Gutenberg himself, ruined by legal disputes, never profited from his own invention. The press hadn't just spread the Reformation; it had made a Reformation of that speed and scale structurally possible for the first time. Frequently asked questions Did Gutenberg invent printing itself? Not entirely — woodblock printing had existed in China and Korea for centuries before Gutenberg, and Korea had even experimented with metal movable type earlier. Gutenberg's specific innovation was a complete, efficient system for European alphabets: durable, precisely-cast reusable metal type, oil-based ink that adhered to metal, and a reliable mechanical press — combined into a practical, scalable process that transformed European printing specifically. Did Gutenberg get rich from his invention? No — one of history's great ironies. His financial backer, Johann Fust, sued him for loan repayment right as his masterwork, the Gutenberg Bible, was nearing completion around 1455, and a court awarded Fust the printing business and equipment. Latin remained an important scholarly language, but printing also encouraged the growth of vernacular literature in languages such as Italian, German, French, Spanish and English. It did not eliminate manuscript culture, which continued for centuries, but it shifted the balance between handwritten and mechanically reproduced texts. passages_top20.text: The printing press changed Europe by dramatically increasing the capacity to reproduce and circulate written and visual information. Before the mid fifteenth century, most European books were copied by hand, which made production relatively slow and expensive. Mechanical printing allowed printers to create multiple copies from the same typeset text, reducing the marginal labour required for additional copies. The technology did not immediately make books cheap or universal, but it changed the economics of publishing and gradually expanded the availability of written material. Printing shops emerged across European cities, producing religious works, classical texts, legal documents, schoolbooks, calendars, pamphlets and commercial information. This increased circulation of texts affected education, religion, scholarship, politics, administration and commerce. The printing press was therefore not merely a faster way to make books; it altered the infrastructure through which European societies produced, preserved and distributed knowledge. Printing had a major effect on Renaissance humanism. Humanist scholars sought manuscripts of Greek and Roman authors, edited texts and circulated their interpretations. Printing did not cause the Reformation by itself because religious disputes, political interests, theological developments and institutional grievances already existed. It nevertheless provided an unusually effective means of spreading arguments across large territories. The ability to reproduce identical or near identical texts helped religious controversies develop beyond local disputes and contributed to the formation of wider confessional communities. Education was transformed gradually as printed textbooks, grammars, dictionaries, theological works and classical texts became more widely available. Universities could use printed editions as teaching resources, while private readers could acquire books for household study. Standardised texts could support more consistent teaching, although editions still contained errors and differences. Printing also encouraged the production of reference works that would have been difficult to reproduce in large numbers by hand. Dictionaries, encyclopaedias, mathematical manuals, medical books and technical instructions could circulate among specialised communities. Increased availability did not mean universal literacy. Reading ability remained strongly influenced by class, gender, occupation and geography, and many people continued to encounter print through public reading or oral communication. question: How did the printing press change Europe?
reference_answer: Johannes Gutenberg's movable-type printing press, developed in Mainz around 1440–1450, let books be mass-produced for the first time and cut the cost of a book by roughly 95% within decades [1]. An estimated 20 million books were printed in Europe by 1500, fueling the spread of literacy, the Protestant Reformation and the Scientific Revolution [1]. Printing spread Martin Luther's 95 Theses across Germany in about two weeks and across Europe within two months, letting reformist ideas outrun the Catholic Church's methods of suppression [3].

Johannes Gutenberg's movable-type printing press, developed in Mainz, Germany around 1440–1450, let books be mass-produced for the first time in history, collapsing the cost of a book by roughly 95% within decades. That triggered an information explosion: an estimated 20 million books were printed in Europe by 1500 alone, fueling the spread of literacy, the Protestant Reformation, and the Scientific Revolution — while Gutenberg himself, ruined by legal disputes, never profited from his own invention. Frequently asked questions Did Gutenberg invent printing itself? Not entirely — woodblock printing had existed in China and Korea for centuries before Gutenberg, and Korea had even experimented with metal movable type earlier. Gutenberg's specific innovation was a complete, efficient system for European alphabets: durable, precisely-cast reusable metal type, oil-based ink that adhered to metal, and a reliable mechanical press — combined into a practical, scalable process that transformed European printing specifically. Did Gutenberg get rich from his invention? No — one of history's great ironies. His financial backer, Johann Fust, sued him for loan repayment right as his masterwork, the Gutenberg Bible, was nearing completion around 1455, and a court awarded Fust the printing business and equipment. Once printing became established, corrected editions of classical works could be reproduced in substantial quantities and distributed across European intellectual networks. Scholars could more easily compare editions and develop shared references to particular texts. Latin remained an important scholarly language, but printing also encouraged the growth of vernacular literature in languages such as Italian, German, French, Spanish and English. Writers could reach audiences beyond their immediate locality. Printing therefore helped transform the intellectual geography of Europe by making scholarly and literary materials more portable and reproducible. It did not eliminate manuscript culture, which continued for centuries, but it shifted the balance between handwritten and mechanically reproduced texts. The printing press was particularly important for religious communication and the Protestant Reformation. Martin Luther's criticisms of Church practices, sermons, theological arguments and translations of biblical material could be reproduced and distributed rapidly through pamphlets, broadsheets and books. Other reformers also used printing to communicate their ideas. Catholic authorities responded with their own printed works, polemics and catechetical materials. passages_top20.text: The printing press changed Europe by dramatically increasing the capacity to reproduce and circulate written and visual information. Before the mid fifteenth century, most European books were copied by hand, which made production relatively slow and expensive. Mechanical printing allowed printers to create multiple copies from the same typeset text, reducing the marginal labour required for additional copies. The technology did not immediately make books cheap or universal, but it changed the economics of publishing and gradually expanded the availability of written material. Printing shops emerged across European cities, producing religious works, classical texts, legal documents, schoolbooks, calendars, pamphlets and commercial information. This increased circulation of texts affected education, religion, scholarship, politics, administration and commerce. The printing press was therefore not merely a faster way to make books; it altered the infrastructure through which European societies produced, preserved and distributed knowledge. Printing had a major effect on Renaissance humanism. Humanist scholars sought manuscripts of Greek and Roman authors, edited texts and circulated their interpretations. Once printing became established, corrected editions of classical works could be reproduced in substantial quantities and distributed across European intellectual networks. Scholars could more easily compare editions and develop shared references to particular texts. Latin remained

The printing press was invented by the German goldsmith Johannes Gutenberg around 1440, and its subsequent global spread revolutionized literary production and communication during the early modern period. Printing did not cause the Reformation by itself because religious disputes, political interests, theological developments and institutional grievances already existed. It nevertheless provided an unusually effective means of spreading arguments across large territories. The ability to reproduce identical or near identical texts helped religious controversies develop beyond local disputes and contributed to the formation of wider confessional communities. Education was transformed gradually as printed textbooks, grammars, dictionaries, theological works and classical texts became more widely available. Universities could use printed editions as teaching resources, while private readers could acquire books for household study. Standardised texts could support more consistent teaching, although editions still contained errors and differences. Printing also encouraged the production of reference works that would have been difficult to reproduce in large numbers by hand. Dictionaries, encyclopaedias, mathematical manuals, medical books and technical instructions could circulate among specialised communities. Increased availability did not mean universal literacy. Reading ability remained strongly influenced by class, gender, occupation and geography, and many people continued to encounter print through public reading or oral communication. question: Why was Canberra chosen as Australia's capital instead of Sydney or Melbourne?
reference_answer: Because of political rivalries between the colonies, some advocates wanted Sydney as the capital while many others wanted Melbourne [5]. To settle the dispute, it was agreed to choose neither city and instead build a new city to be the capital [5]. Canberra was selected as a compromise between Melbourne and Sydney, with its site chosen in 1908 and its designs chosen in 1912 [2][3].

Australia is a country which is below the world, it has beautiful places, many different animals and a lively mix of cultures from its native history and people from all over the world. Important places like Parliament House and the Australian War Memorial are there. Canberra has modern buildings, parks, and cool things to do which makes it a mixture of history, nature, and modern life. Canberra is located in the southeast part of Australia, in its own special area called the Australian Capital Territory. It is bordered by New South Wales to the east and north, while Victoria is to the south. Canberra’s central location within the Australian Capital Territory offers easy access to government institutions and cultural sites. passages_top20.title: What is the Capital of Australia? - Mappr
passages_top20.text: The capital city of Australia is Canberra, and it was founded in 1913. This may come as a surprise to many who are more familiar with the country’s more famous cities: Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane, or Perth. Australia’s capital is located in the northern region of the Australian Capital Territory and is an entirely planned city. The nearest major city is Sydney, which is located approximately 300 kilometers (186 miles) to the north east — Melbourne lies roughly 650 kilometers (404 miles) to the south. Why is Canberra the Capital of Australia? Canberra was chosen as the capital of Australia after a long debate about whether Sydney or Melbourne should be made the capital of the country. As a compromise, it was eventually decided that a capital would be built in the territory of New South Wales, between the two cities, so long as it was at least 160 km (ca. 99 mi) from Sydney. Why Is Sydney Not the Capital City of Australia? Sydney is not the capital of Australia because of political rivalries that existed between colonies. Although there were many advocates for making Sydney the country’s capital, there were also many that wanted the capital to be Melbourne.

passages_top20.title: What is the Capital of Australia? - Mappr
passages_top20.text: The capital city of Australia is Canberra, and it was founded in 1913. This may come as a surprise to many who are more familiar with the country’s more famous cities: Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane, or Perth. Australia’s capital is located in the northern region of the Australian Capital Territory and is an entirely planned city. The nearest major city is Sydney, which is located approximately 300 kilometers (186 miles) to the north east — Melbourne lies roughly 650 kilometers (404 miles) to the south. Why is Canberra the Capital of Australia? Canberra was chosen as the capital of Australia after a long debate about whether Sydney or Melbourne should be made the capital of the country. As a compromise, it was eventually decided that a capital would be built in the territory of New South Wales, between the two cities, so long as it was at least 160 km (ca. 99 mi) from Sydney. Why Is Sydney Not the Capital City of Australia? Sydney is not the capital of Australia because of political rivalries that existed between colonies. Although there were many advocates for making Sydney the country’s capital, there were also many that wanted the capital to be Melbourne.

It is bordered by New South Wales to the east and north, while Victoria is to the south. Canberra’s central location within the Australian Capital Territory offers easy access to government institutions and cultural sites. passages_top20.text: The capital city of Australia is Canberra, and it was founded in 1913. This may come as a surprise to many who are more familiar with the country’s more famous cities: Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane, or Perth. Australia’s capital is located in the northern region of the Australian Capital Territory and is an entirely planned city. The nearest major city is Sydney, which is located approximately 300 kilometers (186 miles) to the north east — Melbourne lies roughly 650 kilometers (404 miles) to the south. Why is Canberra the Capital of Australia? Canberra was chosen as the capital of Australia after a long debate about whether Sydney or Melbourne should be made the capital of the country. As a compromise, it was eventually decided that a capital would be built in the territory of New South Wales, between the two cities, so long as it was at least 160 km (ca. 99 mi) from Sydney. Why Is Sydney Not the Capital City of Australia? Sydney is not the capital of Australia because of political rivalries that existed between colonies. Although there were many advocates for making Sydney the country’s capital, there were also many that wanted the capital to be Melbourne.

Greek theatre is a system that combines architecture, performance, and audience into a single controlled experience. It is not defined by the play itself, but by how space and performance work together to deliver sound, movement, and meaning to a large audience with clarity. This system operates through three connected layers. The structure of the theatre controls visibility and acoustics. Performance techniques—voice, gesture, and masks—extend the actor’s presence across distance. The audience is arranged in a way that ensures a shared and synchronized experience rather than individual interpretation. As a result, performance is not directed at individuals but at the entire space. The audience does not engage privately; it responds collectively within a controlled environment where attention is guided and meaning is reinforced. What defines Greek theatre is this coordination. A single action on stage is designed to reach everyone at once, not through amplification or technology, but through a system that aligns space, movement, and perception. | Element | Role in the System | Effect

Types of Greek Dramas The three genres of drama that emerged during ancient Greece were tragedy, comedy, and satyr plays. Greek Tragedies Tragedy, deriving from the Greek words for “goat” and “song,” dealt with heavy themes, such as murder, vengeance, and betrayal. Most tragedies tended to focus on characters who were legendary heroes or came from royal families. Aristotle, born 384 BCE, spent a great deal of time studying Greek tragedy. Eventually, his analysis culminated in his text, The Poetics, the first substantial work of literary criticism. In his analysis, he presented the argument that poetry and theater could be beneficial to society. He identified six elements that compose every tragedy: plot, character, diction, thought, spectacle, and song. passages_top20.text: Greek Theatre: How Drama, Structure, and Performance Worked Greek theatre was not simply a place for entertainment. It was a structured system designed to control how performance was seen, heard, and experienced by a large audience at once. Every element—from the shape of the seating to the use of masks and voice—worked together to deliver a clear and unified experience. The design of the theatre itself solved practical problems. Thousands of spectators had to see the actors and hear their voices without modern technology. This was achieved through a precise arrangement of space, where seating, stage position, and acoustics were aligned to support performance. Nothing in the structure was accidental. At the same time, performance followed strict conventions. Actors used controlled movement, exaggerated gestures, and vocal projection to match the scale of the space. The audience was not free to interpret randomly; the system guided attention, emotion, and understanding. To understand Greek theatre, it is not enough to know its origins or its famous playwrights. The key is to see how architecture, performance, and audience were integrated into a single system that shaped the entire experience from start to finish. What Is Greek Theatre? passages_top20.text: Ancient Greek Theatre: Origins, Influence, and Legacy Greek theatre, which originated in 6th-century BCE Athens, is one of the most significant cultural legacies of the ancient world. It began with the performance of tragedy plays at religious festivals, particularly those dedicated to Dionysos, the god of wine, fertility, and theatre. These performances inspired the creation of Greek comedy, with both genres becoming immensely popular. They spread across the Mediterranean, influencing Hellenistic and Roman theatre, and continue to inspire contemporary theatre practices and architecture. The Legacy of Ancient Greek Theatre Renowned playwrights such as Sophocles, Euripides, and Aristophanes laid the foundation for what we now recognize as modern theatre. Their works explored themes of morality, human conflict, and the divine, leaving a profound impact on storytelling traditions. The architectural design of ancient Greek theatres, with their open-air structure and exceptional acoustics, remains a model for modern venues worldwide. Visiting historical theatres, such as the Theatre of Dionysus in Athens, provides a unique glimpse into the origins of performance art and storytelling. passages_top20.text: Theatre of ancient Greece A theatrical culture flourished in ancient Greece from 700 BC. At its centre was the city-state of Athens, which became a significant cultural, political, and religious place during this period, and the theatre was institutionalised there as part of a festival called the Dionysia, which honoured the god Dionysus. Tragedy (late 500 BC), comedy (490 BC), and the satyr play were the three dramatic genres emerged there. Athens exported the festival to its numerous colonies. Modern Western theatre comes, in large measure, from the theatre of ancient Greece, from which it borrows technical terminology, classification into genres, and many of its themes, stock characters, and plot elements. Etymology [edit] The word τραγῳδία, tragodia, from which the word "tragedy" is derived, is a compound of two Greek words: τράγος, tragos or "goat" and ᾠδή, ode meaning "song", from ἀείδειν, aeidein, 'to sing'.[1] This etymology indicates a link with the practices of the ancient Dionysian cults. It is impossible, however, to know with certainty how these fertility rituals became the basis for tragedy and comedy.[2] Origins [edit] The Ancient Greeks valued the power of the spoken word, and it was their main method of communication and storytelling. passages_top20.text: Ancient Greek Theatre: Origins, Influence, and Legacy Greek theatre, which originated in 6th-century BCE Athens, is one of the most significant cultural legacies of the ancient world. It began with the performance of tragedy plays at religious festivals, particularly those dedicated to Dionysos, the god of wine, fertility, and theatre. These performances inspired the creation of Greek comedy, with both genres becoming immensely popular. They spread across the Mediterranean, influencing Hellenistic and Roman theatre, and continue to inspire contemporary theatre practices and architecture. The Legacy of Ancient Greek Theatre Renowned playwrights such as Sophocles, Euripides, and Aristophanes laid the foundation for what we now recognize as modern theatre. Their works explored themes of morality, human conflict, and the divine, leaving a profound impact on storytelling traditions. The architectural design of ancient Greek theatres, with their open-air structure and exceptional acoustics, remains a model for modern venues worldwide. Visiting historical theatres, such as the Theatre of Dionysus in Athens, provides a unique glimpse into the origins of performance art and storytelling. passages_top20.text: Theatre of ancient Greece A theatrical culture flourished in ancient Greece from 700 BC. At its centre was the city-state of Athens, which became a significant cultural, political, and religious place during this period, and the theatre was institutionalised there as part of a festival called the Dionysia, which honoured the god Dionysus. Tragedy (late 500 BC), comedy (490 BC), and the satyr play were the three dramatic genres emerged there. Athens exported the festival to its numerous colonies. Modern Western theatre comes, in large measure, from the theatre of ancient Greece, from which it borrows technical terminology, classification into genres, and many of its themes, stock characters, and plot elements. Etymology [edit] The word τραγῳδία, tragodia, from which the word "tragedy" is derived, is a compound of two Greek words: τράγος, tragos or "goat" and ᾠδή, ode meaning "song", from ἀείδειν, aeidein, 'to sing'.[1] This etymology indicates a link with the practices of the ancient Dionysian cults. It is impossible, however, to know with certainty how these fertility rituals became the basis for tragedy and comedy.[2] Origins [edit] The Ancient Greeks valued the power of the spoken word, and it was their main method of communication and storytelling. question: How did ancient Greek theatre work?
reference_answer: Greek theatre worked as a system that combined architecture, performance and audience into a single controlled experience [2]. The theatre's structure controlled visibility and acoustics, projecting sound naturally without microphones, while semicircular seating gave the audience clear visibility [1][2]. Actors used voice, gesture and masks to extend their presence across distance, and masks made characters recognizable to large audiences [1][2]. Performances were tied to city-organized public festivals, especially those dedicated to Dionysus [3].

passages_top20.text: Ancient Greek Theatre: Origins, Influence, and Legacy Greek theatre, which originated in 6th-century BCE Athens, is one of the most significant cultural legacies of the ancient world. It began with the performance of tragedy plays at religious festivals, particularly those dedicated to Dionysos, the god of wine, fertility, and theatre. These performances inspired the creation of Greek comedy, with both genres becoming immensely popular. They spread across the Mediterranean, influencing Hellenistic and Roman theatre, and continue to inspire contemporary theatre practices and architecture. The Legacy of Ancient Greek Theatre Renowned playwrights such as Sophocles, Euripides, and Aristophanes laid the foundation for what we now recognize as modern theatre. Their works explored themes of morality, human conflict, and the divine, leaving a profound impact on storytelling traditions. The architectural design of ancient Greek theatres, with their open-air structure and exceptional acoustics, remains a model for modern venues worldwide. Visiting historical theatres, such as the Theatre of Dionysus in Athens, provides a unique glimpse into the origins of performance art and storytelling. passages_top20.text: Theatre of ancient Greece A theatrical culture flourished in ancient Greece from 700 BC. At its centre was the city-state of Athens, which became a significant cultural, political, and religious place during this period, and the theatre was institutionalised there as part of a festival called the Dionysia, which honoured the god Dionysus. Tragedy (late 500 BC), comedy (490 BC), and the satyr play were the three dramatic genres emerged there. Athens exported the festival to its numerous colonies. Modern Western theatre comes, in large measure, from the theatre of ancient Greece, from which it borrows technical terminology, classification into genres, and many of its themes, stock characters, and plot elements. It is impossible, however, to know with certainty how these fertility rituals became the basis for tragedy and comedy.[2] Origins [edit] The Ancient Greeks valued the power of the spoken word, and it was their main method of communication and storytelling. reference_answer: The Cotswold Games, or Cotswold Olimpick Games, were the first documented modern-era athletic event described as Olympic [1]. Many participants and spectators petitioned for Athens to become the permanent home of the Olympics. Although this idea was not realized, it underscored the importance of Athens in Olympic history. Impact on Modern Olympics The success of the 1896 Olympics proved the viability of the modern Olympic movement. Pierre de Coubertin’s vision gained momentum, and the IOC expanded its influence. Athens’ example set organizational and ceremonial standards that continue to shape the Olympics today. The Games’ emphasis on internationalism, cultural exchange, and athletic excellence became enduring principles. Return of the Olympics to Athens Although Athens did not host the Olympics again until the Intercalated Games of 1906 and later the 2004 Summer Olympics, its role in the history of the Olympics remains unparalleled. The legacy of the 1896 Games is celebrated as the foundation of modern international sports competitions. Twenty-four young men were recruited from the ad—a mix of Stanford students and others in Palo Alto for the summer—and were randomly divided into two groups: prisoners and guards. Why Prisoners Preferred Alcatraz Alcatraz is one of the most notorious prisons in American history, but did it really live up to its feared reputation? A Landmark, Controversial Study On Sunday, August 14, real Palo Alto police officers arrived at the dorms and homes of the prisoners with sirens blaring. They cuffed the prisoners, read them their Miranda rights and booked them at the station on charges of burglary and armed robbery. Then, blindfolded, the students were taken to “prison,” three mocked-up cells in the basement of Jordan Hall on the Stanford campus. What happened in that fake prison over the next six days is the stuff of legend. The Stanford Prison Experiment was supposed to run for two weeks, but Zimbardo had to call it off early when things spiraled out of control.

passages_top20.text: Stanford prison experiment | Stanford prison experiment | | |---|---| | Date | August 14–21, 1971 | |---|---| | Location | | | Also known as | Zimbardo prison experiment SPE ZPE | | Type | Psychological experiment | The Stanford prison experiment (SPE) was a controversial psychological experiment performed in August 1971 at Stanford University. It was designed to be a two-week simulation of a prison environment that examined the effects of situational variables on participants' reactions and behaviors. Stanford psychology professor Philip Zimbardo managed the research team that administered the study.[1] Participants were recruited from the local community through an advertisement in the newspapers offering US$15 (equivalent to $119.25 in 2025) per day to male college students who agreed to participate in a "psychological study of prison life". Twenty-four participants were chosen after assessments of psychological stability and then assigned randomly to the role of prisoners or prison guards.[2] Critics have questioned the validity of these methods.[3] Those volunteers selected to be "guards" were given uniforms designed specifically to de-individuate them, and they were instructed to prevent prisoners from escaping. Its shocking conclusion, that “ordinary college students could do terrible things,” has been used to explain prison riots and abuses at the Abu Ghraib prison in Iraq. It was designed to be a two-week simulation of a prison environment that examined the effects of situational variables on participants' reactions and behaviors. Stanford psychology professor Philip Zimbardo managed the research team that administered the study.[1] Participants were recruited from the local community through an advertisement in the newspapers offering US$15 (equivalent to $119.25 in 2025) per day to male college students who agreed to participate in a "psychological study of prison life". question: What was the Stanford prison experiment?
reference_answer: The Stanford Prison Experiment was a 1971 study run by Stanford psychology professor Philip Zimbardo, in which college students were locked in a fake prison in a basement at Stanford University [3]. Zimbardo wanted to see how people would conform to the roles of prisoner or guard, and whether prison behavior stemmed from personalities or the prison environment [5]. The guards became abusive and authoritarian, while the prisoners became submissive and emotionally distressed [5]. Zimbardo shut it down six days into the planned two weeks [2].

Why Prisoners Preferred Alcatraz Alcatraz is one of the most notorious prisons in American history, but did it really live up to its feared reputation? They cuffed the prisoners, read them their Miranda rights and booked them at the station on charges of burglary and armed robbery. Then, blindfolded, the students were taken to “prison,” three mocked-up cells in the basement of Jordan Hall on the Stanford campus. It was designed to be a two-week simulation of a prison environment that examined the effects of situational variables on participants' reactions and behaviors. Stanford psychology professor Philip Zimbardo managed the research team that administered the study.[1] Participants were recruited from the local community through an advertisement in the newspapers offering US$15 (equivalent to $119.25 in 2025) per day to male college students who agreed to participate in a "psychological study of prison life". Twenty-four participants were chosen after assessments of psychological stability and then assigned randomly to the role of prisoners or prison guards.[2] Critics have questioned the validity of these methods.[3] Those volunteers selected to be "guards" were given uniforms designed specifically to de-individuate them, and they were instructed to prevent prisoners from escaping. Common Causes and Fixes November 1, 2024 Circuit breakers play a crucial role in your home’s electrical system, acting as a safety mechanism to prevent electrical fires and equipment damage. When a circuit breaker trips, it’s doing its job to cut power to a circuit experiencing an issue. But why does this happen? Let’s explore the common causes of tripped circuit breakers and how to address them. Common Causes of Tripped Circuit Breakers - Overloaded Circuits An overloaded circuit is the most frequent reason for a tripped breaker. This happens when the demand for electricity exceeds the circuit’s capacity. For example, plugging too many high-wattage devices into the same outlet can overload the circuit. Signs of an Overload: - Flickering lights - Warm outlets or cords - The breaker trips repeatedly - Short Circuits A short circuit occurs when a hot (live) wire comes into contact with a neutral wire, causing a surge of electricity. This is a serious issue that can result in sparks, smoke, or even fire. Signs of a Short Circuit: - A burning smell near outlets - Scorch marks on outlets or wires - Immediate breaker tripping after resetting - Ground

question: Why do circuit breakers trip?
reference_answer: Circuit breakers trip when they register electrical currents higher than the circuit can handle, cutting off the connection to prevent electrical accidents and damage [1]. Causes include short circuits, grounding faults, arc faults, overloaded circuits and corroded circuits [1]. An overloaded circuit, where demand for electricity exceeds the circuit's capacity, is the most frequent reason [2]. Appliance malfunctions can also trigger a breaker [5].

When a circuit breaker trips, it’s doing its job to cut power to a circuit experiencing an issue. But why does this happen? Common Causes of Tripped Circuit Breakers - Overloaded Circuits An overloaded circuit is the most frequent reason for a tripped breaker. This happens when the demand for electricity exceeds the circuit’s capacity. For example, plugging too many high-wattage devices into the same outlet can overload the circuit. Signs of an Overload: - Flickering lights - Warm outlets or cords - The breaker trips repeatedly - Short Circuits A short circuit occurs when a hot (live) wire comes into contact with a neutral wire, causing a surge of electricity. question: What is the difference between weather and climate?

passages.title: What is the difference between weather and climate?
passages.text: We hear about weather and climate all of the time. Most of us check the local weather forecast to plan our days. And climate change is certainly a “hot” topic in the news. There is, however, still a lot of confusion over the difference between the two. Think about it this way: Climate is what you expect, weather is what you get. Weather is what you see outside on any particular day. So, for example, it may be 75° degrees and sunny or it could be 20° degrees with heavy snow. That’s the weather. Climate is the average of that weather. For example, you can expect snow in the Northeast in January or for it to be hot and humid in the Southeast in July. This is climate. The climate record also includes extreme values such as record high temperatures or record amounts of rainfall. If you’ve ever heard your local weather person say “today we hit a record high for this day,” she is talking about climate records. So when we are talking about climate change, we are talking about changes in long-term averages of daily weather. In most places, weather can change from minute-to-minute, hour-to-hour, day-to-day, and season-to-season.

It is an important consideration in many economic decisions. But what causes it? What are the causes of inflation? Inflation is linked to three factors: demand, supply, and inflation expectations. There can be positive or negative developments in these factors, but generally one or more of these factors is at work when inflation increases or decreases. When these factors are not putting upward or downward pressure on inflation, inflation is equal to its underlying level, which usually measures about 2 percent. Inflation can increase when growing demand outstrips changes in the supply of goods and services. Economists call this “demand-pull inflation.” Another source of higher inflation, known as “cost-push inflation,” occurs when the cost of producing these goods and services rises notably or when they can’t be produced in sufficient quantities to meet demand. Inflation also depends on people’s expectations about where it will be in the future. These expectations influence economic decisions, and this, in turn, affects inflation. However, caffeine does not activate these receptors in the same way adenosine does. Instead, it blocks them. This process is called receptor antagonism. Caffeine does not eliminate the need for sleep or remove the underlying effects of prolonged wakefulness. Caffeine also does not reliably improve complex reasoning, creativity, or decision-making in every situation. Its benefits tend to be most consistent for alertness and vigilance rather than for all forms of intellectual performance. For someone who is well rested, the improvement may be modest. Adenosine is produced as the brain uses energy throughout the day. As it accumulates, it binds to specific proteins called receptors on nerve cells, or neurons. However, caffeine does not activate these receptors in the same way adenosine does. Instead, it blocks them. This process is called receptor antagonism. passages.text: Photosynthesis Photosynthesis[note 1] is a system of biological processes by which photopigment-bearing autotrophic organisms, such as most plants, algae and cyanobacteria, convert light energy—typically from sunlight—into the chemical energy necessary to fuel their metabolism. The term photosynthesis usually refers to oxygenic photosynthesis, a process that releases oxygen as a byproduct of water splitting. Photosynthetic organisms store the converted chemical energy within the bonds of intracellular organic compounds (complex compounds containing carbon), typically carbohydrates like sugars (mainly glucose, fructose and sucrose), starches, phytoglycogen and cellulose. When needing to use this stored energy, an organism's cells then metabolize the organic compounds through cellular respiration. passages.text: Photosynthesis converts sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide into sugar and oxygen through a two-stage process that takes place inside chloroplasts, the green compartments in plant cells. The first stage captures light energy and uses it to split water molecules, releasing oxygen and generating chemical fuel. The second stage spends that fuel to pull carbon dioxide out of the air and stitch it into sugar. The whole operation is more intricate and less efficient than most people assume, and plants have evolved surprisingly varied strategies to cope with its built-in limitations. How Plants Capture Light Chlorophyll, the pigment that makes leaves green, absorbs light most strongly in the red and blue parts of the spectrum and reflects green wavelengths back to your eye. But chlorophyll does not work alone. Accessory pigments, including a second form of chlorophyll and a family of yellow-orange pigments called carotenoids, broaden the range of wavelengths a leaf can harvest. Together, the vibrational and electronic transitions of these pigments can boost light harvesting by two- to four-fold compared to what the main chlorophyll form would capture on its own.1Photochemistry and Photobiology. passages.text: Keyword Search 101: How BM25 Actually Scores The formula in five minutes, then nine things it does that you only see when you measure. BM25 (short for Best Match 25) is the ranking function behind most keyword search: for each word of the query that a document contains, it multiplies how rare the word is across the collection (its IDF, short for inverse document frequency) by how often it appears in the document - a count that saturates and is normalized by the document's length - and adds the results up. Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, Solr, Lucene, Tantivy, Vespa and SQLite's FTS5 all rank with it by default or on request. It's also the oldest part of most modern search stacks - published in 1994, and still the baseline every embedding model is measured against. Most explanations stop at the formula. passages.text: - Share What Causes Inflation? Inflation is the sustained rise in the general level of the prices of goods and services in an economy over time. It is an important consideration in many economic decisions. But what causes it? What are the causes of inflation? Inflation is linked to three factors: demand, supply, and inflation expectations. There can be positive or negative developments in these factors, but generally one or more of these factors is at work when inflation increases or decreases. When these factors are not putting upward or downward pressure on inflation, inflation is equal to its underlying level, which usually measures about 2 percent. Inflation can increase when growing demand outstrips changes in the supply of goods and services. Economists call this “demand-pull inflation.” Another source of higher inflation, known as “cost-push inflation,” occurs when the cost of producing these goods and services rises notably or when they can’t be produced in sufficient quantities to meet demand. Inflation also depends on people’s expectations about where it will be in the future. These expectations influence economic decisions, and this, in turn, affects inflation. Other people find that their eyes get less irritated if they run water while they’re cutting onions. Protect yourself from vapors Try running a fan to circulate the air or wearing eye protection, such as goggles, while you prepare onions. Working under a cooking hood, which supplies ventilation, may also help. One old tale says to keep a piece of white bread in your mouth while cutting, based on the theory that the bread will absorb onion vapor. There’s no evidence for this, but it’s worth a shot. The distinctive taste of fresh onion can be hard to replicate. But you may want to substitute onions in your cooking if they frequently cause uncomfortable, disruptive eye symptoms. Fresher onions are less likely to cause crying than those that have been stored for an extended period of time. Here are some other tips for preventing crying from cutting onions: Cut your onions properly The way you cut onions may help reduce crying to some extent. Some chefs recommend slicing away from you so that the onion vapor doesn’t rise directly into your eyes. However you slice them, try to avoid cutting your onion near the root end. This is the part that contains the highest concentration of sulfuric compounds that can make you cry. Using a sharp knife may also help. The sharper the knife, the less damage is done to the onion, and fewer irritations are released into the air as a result. Use water To reduce or eliminate onion tears, you may have the best luck if you diminish the sulfuric acid compounds in the onion itself. Garlic belongs to the same family and carries the alliinase enzyme, but it lacks lachrymatory factor synthase entirely, so it can never brew the syn-propanethial-S-oxide that an onion does. Chop a whole bulb of garlic and your eyes stay dry. Why Do Raw Onions Burn Your Mouth? The same chemical machinery that ambushes your eyes also goes after your mouth, just by a slightly different route. When you bite into a raw onion, you rupture exactly the same cells, and the alliinase enzyme meets the amino acid sulfoxides to spawn those unstable sulfenic acids. This time, though, they rearrange into a family of sharp sulfur compounds called thiosulfinates, the molecules responsible for the characteristic bite and pungency of a raw onion. These compounds irritate the free nerve endings in your mouth and on your tongue, the same kind of warning sensors that flag the heat of a chili pepper.
